strategies.summary: Implement a custom CUDA forward path that computes QK^T scaling, row-wise stable softmax, and AV in one streamed kernel pipeline to reduce global memory traffic versus materializing the attention matrix.
implementation_hints: Export a single entrypoint from cuda_cpp and dispatch to a CUDA wrapper in cuda_cu while keeping ModelNew I/O unchanged.
Use a tiled online-softmax style algorithm: accumulate per-row max and normalization while iterating over K/V tiles, then finalize weighted V accumulation without storing full attention scores.
Parallelize across batch/head/query rows; map threads to contiguous head-dim or value-dim fragments for coalesced Q/K/V reads.
Preserve exact semantic order: dot-product -> scaling -> masking if later added -> softmax over key axis -> weighted sum over V.
strategies.expected_gain: High for moderate-to-long sequence lengths due to avoiding large intermediate attention tensors and reducing DRAM bandwidth pressure.
risk_notes: Numerical stability is critical; use row-wise max/sum accumulation and avoid changing the softmax axis.
Need to validate shape/layout assumptions carefully because the scaffold exposes only Q/K/V tensors and no explicit mask argument.
Level-1 scope may favor a simpler forward-only kernel; overly aggressive fusion can increase implementation complexity.

review_notes.openai-compatible: High upside and strong semantic fit. A streamed fused CUDA forward path with online softmax directly targets the main bandwidth bottleneck while preserving required Q/K/V, scaling, masking, and softmax ordering. Risk is meaningful due to implementation complexity and numerical-stability details, but risk-adjusted value is still excellent for this workload.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Strong, well-scoped Flash Attention-style online softmax kernel. Targets the right anchors, avoids materializing the full attention matrix, and explicitly preserves semantic order. High expected gain for moderate-to-long sequences. Risk is manageable with careful numerical stability handling. Best overall candidate.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Excellent approach. Implementing a fused FlashAttention-style kernel with online softmax is the standard and most effective way to optimize scaled dot-product attention in CUDA.

strategies.summary: Implement a fused Flash Attention kernel in CUDA that computes QK^T scaling, softmax, and weighted sum of V in a single tiled pass, avoiding materialization of the full attention matrix.
implementation_hints: Implement a Flash Attention v2-style kernel: tile over Q rows and K/V columns, accumulate softmax numerator and denominator on-the-fly using the online softmax trick (track running max and sum per row).
Each CUDA block handles one (batch, head) pair and a tile of Q rows; threads within a block cooperate over K/V tiles using shared memory.
Scale QK dot products by 1/sqrt(d_k) before softmax; use __expf for speed with --use_fast_math.
Export a C++ wrapper via pybind11 that accepts Q, K, V tensors (float32, contiguous, shape [B, H, S, D]) and returns the output tensor.
In forward_stmt_1, call _stark_get_extension().flash_attn_forward(Q, K, V) replacing the PyTorch fallback.
Use shared memory for Q tile, K tile, and V tile; tune tile sizes (e.g., 64x64) to fit in shared memory for typical head dims (64, 128).
Handle the causal mask optionally by skipping upper-triangular K/V tiles.
strategies.expected_gain: 2-4x speedup over PyTorch sdpa baseline for typical (B, H, S, D) shapes by eliminating HBM round-trips for the attention matrix.
risk_notes: Numerical stability requires careful online softmax implementation; test against PyTorch reference with atol=1e-3.
Shared memory usage must be within device limits; parameterize tile size based on head dim.
Only handles float32 initially; bfloat16/float16 require separate handling.
Assumes contiguous input tensors; add .contiguous() calls in the Python wrapper.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Also high-upside and technically sound, but more prescriptive and higher risk than strategy_01 because it assumes a fairly specific FlashAttention-v2 style implementation, float32-only wrapper details, contiguous layout assumptions, and use of fast math. Strong candidate, but slightly less robust on risk-adjusted grounds.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Detailed Flash Attention v2 implementation plan with concrete tiling strategy, shared memory usage, pybind11 wiring, and forward call site integration. Covers dtype, contiguity, and tile size concerns. Slightly higher implementation complexity than strategy_01 but very well specified. Top-tier candidate.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Highly detailed and accurate strategy for implementing FlashAttention v2. The use of shared memory and online softmax is critical for performance and numerical stability.

strategies.summary: Implement a block-tiled fused attention kernel (FlashAttention style) in CUDA using shared memory and online softmax.
implementation_hints: Tile Q, K, and V tensors into shared memory blocks to maximize data reuse.
For each block of Q, iterate over blocks of K and V.
Compute QK^T, scale by 1/sqrt(d), and use the online softmax algorithm (maintaining running max and sum) to ensure numerical stability without materializing the full attention matrix.
Multiply the softmax weights with V and accumulate the result in registers before writing to global memory.
strategies.expected_gain: Significant reduction in memory bandwidth and latency by avoiding the materialization of the O(N^2) intermediate attention matrix.
risk_notes: Shared memory capacity limits may restrict block sizes.
Numerical stability of the online softmax requires careful implementation.
Handling sequence lengths that are not perfectly divisible by the block size.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Solid kernel-level direction with good alignment to attention semantics and likely performance gains from shared-memory tiling plus online softmax. Slightly lower risk-adjusted value than strategy_01 because it is less explicit about wrapper/fallback integration and broader shape-handling concerns.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Solid FlashAttention-style tiled kernel targeting cuda_cu. Covers online softmax, shared memory tiling, and avoids O(N^2) materialization. Slightly less detailed than strategy_02 on wiring and edge cases, but a strong kernel implementation plan. Good risk-adjusted value.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Strong core CUDA strategy. Block-tiling and online softmax are exactly what is needed to avoid O(N^2) memory materialization.

strategies.summary: Add a fast-path CUDA kernel specialized for common contiguous tensor layouts and dtypes, while retaining fallback to torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention for unsupported cases.
implementation_hints: In forward_stmt_1, gate the extension call on CUDA device, contiguity, supported dtype, and expected rank/layout; otherwise preserve the baseline PyTorch path.
In cuda_cu, assume a narrow set of layouts such as [B,H,L,D] contiguous or equivalent flattened strides to simplify indexing and improve occupancy.
Use helpers only to keep extension build/load behavior unchanged; avoid init_body changes unless caching metadata is clearly beneficial.
Keep the exported ABI minimal: one forward entrypoint with internal checks and descriptive failure behavior.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate, by enabling an optimized kernel on the hot path without regressing correctness on edge cases.
risk_notes: Stride/layout mismatches are a common source of silent errors; validate tensor assumptions before launching.
Fallback coverage is essential to preserve semantics for unsupported dtypes or noncontiguous inputs.
Fast-path specialization may miss some benchmark variants if shape assumptions are too narrow.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Very strong risk-adjusted strategy. A specialized CUDA fast path with explicit fallback preserves correctness for unsupported layouts/dtypes while still enabling meaningful acceleration on the hot path. This is pragmatic, benchmark-friendly, and reduces the chance of semantic regressions.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Defensive fast-path with fallback to PyTorch SDPA. Useful for robustness and correctness coverage on edge cases, but the fallback design limits peak performance gains. Good as a safety net or complement to aggressive fusion strategies, but not a primary optimization driver.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Good engineering practice to include a fallback to PyTorch's native SDPA for unsupported shapes, dtypes, or non-contiguous layouts.

strategies.summary: Implement a vectorized tiled softmax+matmul kernel using float4 loads and warp-level parallelism to maximize memory throughput for the attention computation.
implementation_hints: Write a CUDA kernel that processes the attention computation with vectorized float4 memory accesses for Q, K, V tensors to maximize memory bandwidth.
Assign one warp per query token; each warp iterates over all key tokens, accumulates dot products, applies online softmax, and accumulates the V-weighted output.
Use __ldg() for read-only cache hints on K and V tensors.
Tile the K/V iteration in registers to reduce shared memory pressure; store partial sums in registers.
Export via pybind11 with input validation (contiguous, float32, 4D tensors).
Launch with grid=(batch*heads, num_query_tiles) and block=(warp_size * warps_per_block).
strategies.expected_gain: 1.5-2.5x speedup for small to medium sequence lengths by improving memory access patterns and reducing kernel launch overhead.
risk_notes: float4 loads require 16-byte alignment; verify tensor strides.
Warp-per-query approach may underutilize GPU for very short sequences.
Online softmax with warp shuffles requires careful implementation to avoid numerical issues.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Potentially good for certain aligned shapes and smaller-to-medium sequence lengths, but more brittle than broader tiled fused approaches. Alignment constraints, warp-mapping assumptions, and numerical-softmax complexity reduce robustness, so the risk-adjusted value is moderate.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Vectorized float4 + warp-per-query approach is a practical alternative to full Flash Attention, especially for smaller sequence lengths. Concrete implementation hints (float4, __ldg, warp shuffles). Alignment and warp underutilization risks are real but manageable. Good risk-adjusted value for medium-scale workloads.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Good low-level optimization details, particularly the use of float4 vectorized loads and warp-level parallelism.

strategies.summary: Use backend-level vectorization and shared-memory tiling around head dimension/value dimension to improve arithmetic intensity within the custom attention kernel.
implementation_hints: Tile K and V into shared memory per block so multiple query rows reuse the same key/value data.
Vectorize loads/stores where alignment permits, especially along the innermost head/value dimensions, to improve memory throughput.
Choose tile sizes that balance shared-memory usage and occupancy; prefer simple static configurations suitable for Level-1 benchmarks.
Keep launch wiring and exported wrapper signatures localized to cuda_cpp/cuda_cu.
strategies.expected_gain: Moderate to high when head_dim is favorable for vectorized memory access and sequence tiles can be effectively reused.
risk_notes: Shared-memory pressure can reduce occupancy if tile sizes are too large.
Vectorization must respect alignment and tail handling to avoid incorrect reads.
These low-level optimizations should not alter Q/K/V ordering or softmax normalization behavior.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Good lower-level optimization layer to pair with a fused attention kernel. Vectorization and shared-memory tiling can help materially when head/value dimensions are favorable. Slightly less complete as a top-level strategy because it depends on a sound kernel structure already being in place.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Generic shared-memory tiling and vectorization guidance targeting cuda_cu/cuda_cpp. Reasonable but less specific than strategy_02 or strategy_07. Lacks concrete tile size recommendations or online softmax details. Moderate value as a supplementary optimization direction.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Solid advice on vectorization and shared memory tiling to maximize arithmetic intensity.

Allocate the output tensor with the same shape as Q.
Calculate the appropriate grid and block dimensions based on the sequence length and head dimension.
Launch the CUDA kernel and expose the function to Python via PYBIND11_MODULE.

risk_notes: Must ensure inputs are contiguous or handle strides correctly in the kernel.

Good companion strategy, though risk-adjusted usefulness is modest because it does not itself improve algorithmic efficiency and mainly supports other kernel strategies.

review_notes.gemini-compatible: Necessary C++ boilerplate for exposing the CUDA kernel to PyTorch. Standard and correct.

strategies.summary: Delegate to cuBLAS for batched GEMM (QK^T) and use a custom CUDA kernel for row-wise softmax and V weighting, keeping correctness while improving memory bandwidth utilization.
implementation_hints: Use torch.ops or cublasSgemmStridedBatched via ATen's mm for the QK^T batched matmul, then apply a custom CUDA softmax kernel, then another batched matmul for the V weighting.
Write a custom row-wise softmax kernel using warp-level reductions (warp shuffle instructions) for the softmax over the sequence dimension.
Scale Q by 1/sqrt(d_k) before the matmul to avoid a separate scaling kernel.
Export the softmax kernel via pybind11; keep the two matmuls as torch operations in forward_stmt_1 to leverage cuBLAS.
Use __shfl_down_sync for warp reductions in the softmax kernel to minimize shared memory usage.
strategies.expected_gain: 1.5-2x speedup over naive PyTorch by using a faster softmax kernel; less gain than full Flash Attention due to HBM materialization of attention weights.
risk_notes: Materializing the full S×S attention matrix limits scalability for long sequences.
Must preserve softmax axis (over key dimension, axis=-1).
Warp reduction assumes sequence length is a multiple of warp size; add padding or masking for edge cases.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Moderate value. Leveraging GEMM libraries reduces kernel-writing burden and likely improves over naive implementations, but materializing the attention matrix leaves major performance on the table for longer sequences. Safer than full fusion, but lower ceiling and weaker scalability.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Hybrid cuBLAS + custom softmax approach. Materializes the full S×S attention matrix, limiting scalability and memory efficiency. The custom softmax kernel adds complexity without the full benefit of Flash Attention. Warp reduction edge cases add risk. Lower value compared to full fusion strategies.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Suboptimal. Materializing the attention matrix to use cuBLAS defeats the primary memory-bandwidth benefits of a fused SDPA kernel.

implementation_hints: In forward_stmt_1, use torch.backends.cuda.sdp_kernel context manager to force flash_sdp_enabled=True and math_sdp_enabled=False, ensuring the Flash Attention CUDA kernel path is taken.
Wrap the sdpa call inside the context manager in forward_stmt_1.
In helpers, add a check at module load time that flash SDP is available (torch.backends.cuda.flash_sdp_enabled()) and fall back gracefully.
This avoids writing a custom kernel while still getting Flash Attention performance from PyTorch's built-in implementation.
Ensure Q, K, V are in float16 or bfloat16 if Flash Attention requires it; add dtype casting in forward_stmt_1 if needed.
strategies.expected_gain: 1.5-3x speedup by ensuring Flash Attention backend is used instead of the math (naive) backend, with no custom kernel risk.
risk_notes: Flash Attention in PyTorch requires float16 or bfloat16; float32 inputs may fall back to math backend.
Availability depends on GPU architecture (Ampere+ for best results).
dtype casting introduces overhead and potential precision loss.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Attractive for low engineering effort, but its usefulness depends heavily on dtype, architecture, and whether the existing baseline already routes to an efficient SDPA backend. Explicit backend forcing may help in some cases, yet it offers less controllable and less portable value than a dedicated custom fast path.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Relies on PyTorch's built-in Flash Attention via sdp_kernel context manager. Zero custom kernel risk, but float32 inputs (common in L1 benchmarks) will likely fall back to the math backend, negating the benefit. dtype casting overhead and architecture dependency further reduce reliability. Low risk-adjusted value for this task.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Violates the spirit of the task. KernelBench Level 1 expects a custom CUDA kernel implementation, not just wrapping PyTorch's built-in SDPA with a context manager.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

# <<<IMPROVE:helpers>>>
_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l1_p97_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():
    global _STARK_EXTENSION
    if _STARK_EXTENSION is None:
        _STARK_EXTENSION = load_inline(
            name=_stark_extension_name(),
            cpp_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC),
            cuda_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC),
            functions=None,
            extra_cflags=['-O3'],
            extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3', '--use_fast_math'],
            with_cuda=True,
            verbose=False,
        )
    return _STARK_EXTENSION
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

CUDA_CPP_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cpp>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>

// Add pybind exports for custom CUDA entrypoints here.
PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) {}
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

CUDA_CU_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cu>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>
#include <cuda.h>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Add CUDA kernels and exported wrapper functions here.
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

class ModelNew(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # <<<IMPROVE:init_body>>>
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

    def forward(self, Q: torch.Tensor, K: torch.Tensor, V: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_1>>>
        # Baseline fallback keeps the official PyTorch forward path.
        # After implementing CUDA_CPP_SRC / CUDA_CU_SRC, call _stark_get_extension().your_entrypoint(...).
        out = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_2>>>
        return out
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
